12550:
A possibility is something that can happen, can exist, or can be true — it has not been ruled out, but it also has not been confirmed.

Think of the space between two extremes:

  • Certain → it will definitely happen
  • Impossible → it absolutely cannot happen

A possibility lives between those two poles. It's a candidate. It's eligible. Nothing blocks it from happening, even if nothing guarantees it either.

"It's a possibility that I'll get the job."

This means: I could get the job. It hasn't happened. It might not happen. But it's also not impossible. It's in play.

For something to be a possibility, two conditions must be true:

  1. Nothing rules it out. The laws of nature, the facts of the situation, or the rules in place don't make it impossible.
  2. It hasn't been decided yet. There is still uncertainty about whether it will happen.

Examples:

  • "Rain tomorrow is a possibility." → Weather conditions allow it. It hasn't happened yet.
  • "Becoming a doctor is a possibility for her." → She has the academic background. Nothing stops her.
  • "It is not a possibility to travel faster than light." → Physics rules it out entirely. So it has no possibility at all.

This is one of the most important things to understand: a possibility can be very unlikely, and still be a possibility.

All of these are possibilities:

  • Winning the lottery (very unlikely)
  • Getting a cold this winter (quite likely)
  • Meeting a famous celebrity today (rare, but can happen)

They are all possibilities because none of them is impossible. The word says nothing about how probable something is — only that it can happen.

When you want to say how likely something is, you use words like probability, chance, or likelihood. But possibility just asks the simpler question: Can it happen at all?

Even though "possibility" doesn't mean likely, we often use describing words with it to indicate how strong or weak it is:

  • "A remote possibility" — It can happen, but barely. Very unlikely.
    "There's a remote possibility the flight leaves on time in this storm."
  • "A real possibility" — It's genuinely plausible. Take it seriously.
    "Losing the match is a real possibility if we don't prepare."
  • "A strong possibility" — It's quite likely to happen.
    "She's a strong possibility for the promotion."
  • "A distinct possibility" — It clearly could happen; don't dismiss it.
    "The project going over budget is a distinct possibility."

In each case, the word possibility itself just means "can happen" — the adjective tells you how likely.

When used in the plural — possibilities — the word often shifts slightly in meaning. It refers to the options, choices, or paths available to you in a situation.

"We have several possibilities: take the train, drive, or fly."

Here, possibilities = the choices you can make. Each one is available; none is blocked. This use is very common in everyday speech:

  • "Let's explore all the possibilities before we decide."
  • "I've been thinking about the possibilities, and I think we should move."
  • "The possibilities are endless." (Meaning: there are many ways things could go or many things you could do.)

"Possibility" also carries a more abstract, philosophical, even emotional meaning — the sense of openness about the future, of things that could be achieved or experienced.

"She moved to the new city full of excitement, seeing possibilities everywhere."

This doesn't mean specific options. It means she felt that the future was open, unwritten, and full of things that could happen for her. It's the feeling that doors are not yet closed.

This is why the word is often used in uplifting or motivational contexts:

  • "Don't close your mind to new possibilities."
  • "The discovery opened up exciting possibilities for science."
  • "As a child, life felt like a world of infinite possibilities."

In this sense, "possibilities" represents the richness of what could be — not what is, but what could become.

These words are close cousins, but each has a distinct role:

Possibility vs. Probability / Likelihood

  • Possibility = can it happen? (yes or no)
  • Probability = how likely is it to happen? (a matter of degree)

Something can be a possibility with almost zero probability. "Winning the lottery is a possibility, but the probability is extremely low."

Possibility vs. Opportunity

  • An opportunity is a favorable, often time-limited chance that invites you to act. It usually implies something good and something you should consider doing.
  • A possibility is neutral. It just means something can happen. It doesn't call you to action.

"There's a possibility it will rain." — A neutral fact.
"This is an opportunity to learn from a great teacher." — A favorable opening you should consider taking.

Possibility vs. Chance
These two are very close in everyday use, and people often use them interchangeably. The subtle difference: chance often implies an element of luck or randomness, while possibility focuses on whether something is within the range of what can occur. But in most situations, "there's a chance" and "there's a possibility" mean the same thing.

Possibility vs. Ability

  • Ability is about what a person or thing is capable of doing — their personal power or skill.
  • Possibility is about whether something can happen, given all the circumstances.

"She has the ability to finish the project." → She has the skill.
"It's a possibility that she'll finish it today." → It could happen, depending on everything.

"Possibility" works both ways grammatically, and the meaning shifts slightly:

As a countable noun (you can count specific possibilities):

  • "There is a possibility that he won't come." (one specific scenario that might be true)
  • "We discussed three possibilities." (three distinct options)
  • "I see two possibilities here."

As an uncountable noun (talking about possibility in general, as a concept):

  • "Is there any possibility of getting a refund?" (Can it happen at all?)
  • "There is no possibility of changing the date." (It cannot happen.)
  • "Beyond the realm of possibility." (Outside what is achievable.)

When you say "no possibility," you're saying the door is completely shut — it cannot happen.

"Within the realm of possibility"
Something that is realistic and achievable.
"Finishing the book this year is within the realm of possibility."

"Outside the realm of possibility" / "Beyond the realm of possibility"
Something that cannot happen; it's too extreme or impossible.
"Teleporting to work is outside the realm of possibility."

"Leave open the possibility"
To not rule something out; to keep it as a candidate.
"The doctor left open the possibility that it might resolve on its own."

"Rule out the possibility"
To decide something cannot happen or is not viable.
"The police have not ruled out the possibility of foul play."

"Explore the possibilities"
To consider the available options.
"Before deciding, let's explore all the possibilities."

"Open up new possibilities"
To create new options that didn't exist before.
"The new law opens up new possibilities for small businesses."

Possibility means: something that can happen, can be true, or can be chosen — something that has not been ruled out.

It asks the question: Is this door open? If yes — it's a possibility.

It does not ask: Will it happen? Is it likely? Those are questions of probability, not possibility.

In its plural form (possibilities), it usually means the options or paths available to you. In its more abstract use, it captures the open, hopeful sense of a future where things can still go many ways.

The word is simple in concept but rich in use — from logical statements ("there is no possibility of error") to emotional ones ("the city felt full of possibilities") to practical ones ("let's explore our possibilities"). Once you see that the thread connecting all these uses is the same — can this happen? — the word becomes clear in every context.
12551:
Posterity means all the people who will live after us in the future — every generation that comes after the current one. It refers to future human beings as a whole group, not any one specific person.

Think of it like a long river of time. You are standing somewhere in the middle of that river. Everyone who already lived is behind you (the past). Posterity is everyone who will exist ahead of you — your children, their children, their grandchildren, and every human being who will ever be born after this moment, stretching far into the future.

Posterity is a collective noun, meaning it refers to a group as a single unit — much like how "humanity" means all humans together, not just one person. You wouldn't say "a posterity" or "three posterities." You simply say posterity, and it means all future generations bundled together as one idea.

✅ "We must protect the forests for posterity."
❌ "We must protect the forests for a posterity."

1. Posterity = All Future Generations (General)

In this sense, posterity means the whole of humanity that is yet to come — not your personal family, but everyone who will ever live after us.

"These ancient cave paintings were preserved so that posterity could understand how early humans lived."

Here, "posterity" means people living thousands of years from now who will study these paintings.

"The decisions we make today about climate change will affect posterity for centuries."

2. Posterity = One's Own Descendants (Personal)

Sometimes, posterity is used more personally to mean your own future family line — your children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and so on.

"The king built a vast empire, hoping to leave a lasting legacy for his posterity."

Here it means his own bloodline and heirs, not all of humanity.

Both uses are correct. Context tells you which one is meant, but both carry the same basic idea: people who come after.

By far the most common way you will encounter this word is in the phrase "for posterity." This phrase means: doing or saving something so that future generations will have it, remember it, or benefit from it.

It carries the idea that something is worth preserving across time.

"The interview was recorded for posterity." (= so future people can watch it and remember this moment)

"She kept all of her grandfather's letters for posterity." (= so the family's future generations would have them)

"Let's take a photo for posterity!" (= so we have a record of this moment to look back on)

This phrase is also sometimes used with light humor in everyday speech — someone might say "let's save this embarrassing video for posterity" as a joke, playing on the grand, serious tone of the word.

Posterity is a formal and somewhat solemn word. It carries a sense of weight and importance. When someone uses it, they are usually trying to say that something matters beyond the present moment — that it has significance that will echo through time.

You'll most often find it in:

  • Historical writing and speeches
  • Philosophy and literature
  • Serious journalism
  • Legal and political documents

It is not a casual, everyday word. You wouldn't normally hear it in informal conversation. But understanding it helps you read serious texts more deeply.

This is worth being clear about, because the word can seem slippery:

  • It does not refer to the past. The opposite of posterity — people who lived before us — are called our ancestors, forebears, or predecessors.
  • It does not refer to the present. It strictly means future people.
  • It is not a synonym for "popularity" or "fame." Those are unrelated words. Posterity is purely about future generations of people, not about how well-known something is.

Here are a few more sentences to sharpen your feel for the word:

"Abraham Lincoln's speeches were written not just for his time, but for posterity."

"Will posterity judge us kindly for how we treated the planet?"

"The scientist published her findings so that posterity might build upon her work."

"He had no children and worried about what he would leave behind for posterity."

If you ever need to recall this word instantly, remember this:

Posterity = all the people who will live after us, especially as the audience or inheritors of what we do today.

It is the idea that our actions, creations, and choices outlive us — and that the people of the future are watching, even if they haven't been born yet.
12552:
Posthumous is an adjective that describes something that happens, is given, or comes into existence after a person has died.

The most important thing to lock in your mind is this: it is entirely about timing. Specifically, the timing of an event in relation to a person's death. If something happens while a person is still alive, it cannot be called posthumous. If it happens after they have died, it can be.

The word is never used on its own to describe a person. It always describes a thing — an award, a book, a child, a reputation — that is connected to someone who has since passed away.

1. Posthumous Awards and Honors

This is the most frequent way you will encounter this word. When a person dies and then receives an award, medal, honorary degree, or any kind of official recognition, that recognition is called posthumous.

A soldier dies bravely in battle. His country later awards him its highest military honor. Since he is no longer alive to receive it, the award is posthumous. His family accepts it on his behalf.

A scientist spends her life doing groundbreaking research but never wins the Nobel Prize. After she dies, the Nobel committee recognizes her contributions and awards it to her. It is a posthumous Nobel Prize.

The key point: the person did something worthy during their life. But the formal recognition came after their death. That gap is exactly what "posthumous" captures.

2. Posthumous Publications and Creative Works

When an author, musician, artist, or filmmaker dies, they often leave behind unfinished or unpublished work. If that work is later released to the public after their death, it is called a posthumous work, album, novel, painting collection, and so on.

A poet dies leaving behind hundreds of unpublished poems in a drawer. A decade later, a publisher collects them into a book. That book is a posthumous publication.

A musician records songs that never made it onto an album. After they die, their record label puts those recordings together and releases them. That album is a posthumous release.

This use is extremely common in art and literature. Many famous works were only shared with the world after their creator's death.

3. Posthumous Fame and Reputation

Some people are largely unknown or underappreciated while they are alive, and only become celebrated after their death. Their fame, in such cases, is posthumous.

The painter Vincent van Gogh sold almost no paintings during his lifetime and lived in poverty. After his death, he became one of the most celebrated artists in history. His fame was entirely posthumous.

4. A Posthumous Child

This is a less common but historically important use of the word. A child who is born after their father has died is traditionally referred to as a posthumous child. The father never got to meet them.

A soldier goes to war, and his wife is pregnant. He is killed before the baby is born. The baby, once born, is called a posthumous child.

This is the only case where the word connects to a living person (the child), because the child's very existence as a recognized child of the father came into being only after the father's death.

It is worth clearing up what this word does not mean, because learners sometimes confuse it with related ideas.

  • It does not mean "tragic" or "sad." A posthumous award is simply one that was given after death. It carries no built-in tone of sadness, though the circumstances may naturally feel that way.
  • It does not mean "forgotten." A posthumous reputation can be enormous and celebrated.
  • It does not mean something happened a long time ago. A person could die today and receive a posthumous award tomorrow. The gap in time can be very short or very long.
  • It does not describe the quality of the work. A posthumous novel is not necessarily better or worse than the author's other work — it simply came out after they died.
A Simple Test to Use This Word Correctly

Ask yourself two questions:

  1. Is the person dead? ✅
  2. Did the thing (the award, the book, the child, the recognition) come after their death? ✅

If both answers are yes, the word posthumous fits perfectly.

If the person was still alive when the thing happened, you cannot use this word, no matter how meaningful or important the event was.

Posthumous means occurring or continuing after a person's death. It is used to describe awards, works of art, publications, fame, children, and any event or outcome that is connected to a specific person but that happened only once that person was no longer alive. The word says nothing about how good, important, or sad something is — it only tells you when it happened: after death.
12553: "Posthumously" means after the death of the person it concerns. When something happens posthumously, it happens after a specific person has died — and that thing is directly connected to that person.
The core idea

Think of it this way: something is done for someone, about someone, or credited to someone — but only after that person is no longer alive.

Two things must be true for this word to apply:

  • The person has already died.
  • Something related specifically to that person happens after their death.

It is not just any event that happens after someone dies. It must be tied directly to the dead person — an award they receive, a book they wrote that gets published, fame they earn, a pardon they are granted, and so on.
The most common situations where you'll see this word
1. Awards and honours

This is the most frequent use of "posthumously." When a person dies before receiving an award, or when an award is given in recognition of their life's work after they have died, it is said to be awarded posthumously.

"The soldier was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor."

He had already died in battle. The medal was presented to his family at a ceremony after his death. He himself never held it.

"She was posthumously given the Nobel Prize."

The prize committee recognized her work only after she had passed away.
2. Books, music, films, and other creative work

When a writer, musician, or artist dies before their work is published, released, or shown to the world, that work reaches the public posthumously.

"Her novel was published posthumously."

She finished writing it during her lifetime, but died before anyone could read it in print.

"Several of Mozart's compositions were performed posthumously."

He died young, and some of his music was heard by audiences only after his death.
3. Fame and recognition

Sometimes a person receives no attention or appreciation during their lifetime, but becomes celebrated or respected only after dying. That recognition arrives posthumously.

"Van Gogh achieved his fame posthumously — he sold almost no paintings while he was alive."

Today he is one of the most recognized artists in history, but he died in poverty and obscurity. The world noticed him only after he was gone.
4. Legal actions — pardons, convictions, and rulings

Sometimes a government, court, or authority takes an official legal action that applies to a person who has already died.

"She was posthumously pardoned by the government for a crime she did not commit."

The pardon came too late for her. She had already served her punishment and died. But the record was officially corrected after her death.

"He was posthumously convicted based on evidence discovered years later."

He died before the investigation was complete, but the legal finding was made after his death.
5. Being born posthumously

This is a special and older use of the word. A child is described as born posthumously when their father died before the child was born. Since the father never lived to see the birth, the child's birth happened after their father's death.

"He never met his son, who was born posthumously."
What "posthumously" does NOT mean

It does not simply mean "something that happens after a person dies" in a general sense. If a person dies and then a war breaks out in their country, you would not say the war happened "posthumously." The event must have a direct connection to — or be done specifically in relation to — the person who has died.

The word is always about the relationship between the event and the deceased person. Take away that connection, and the word no longer applies.
The emotional weight of this word

There is something quietly sorrowful about "posthumously." When something happens posthumously, the one person it most concerns can never experience it, witness it, or feel it. They will never know they won the award. They will never see their book on a shelf. They will never hear the applause.

This is what often makes posthumous recognition bittersweet. It is meaningful — the truth is acknowledged, the talent is honoured, the injustice is corrected — but the person who perhaps deserved it most is no longer there to receive it.
A set of examples to lock it in

• "The director was posthumously awarded an honorary Oscar at the ceremony." — He had died before the award was announced.
  • "Her diaries were published posthumously by her family." — She kept them private during her life; the world read them only after she was gone.
  • "The government posthumously restored his reputation." — He was falsely accused. Only after his death did the truth come out.
  • "Beethoven's Tenth Symphony was completed and performed posthumously by scholars." — He left sketches; others finished the work after he died.
  • "The medal was posthumously awarded to the firefighter who died saving others." — The honour came after the sacrifice.
One sentence to remember it by
Whenever you see "posthumously," ask yourself: "Who has died, and what is being done for them — or about them — now that they are gone?" That is always what the word is pointing to.
12554: A postmaster is a person who is officially in charge of a post office. Think of them as the manager — the person responsible for making sure everything inside a post office runs smoothly.

A postmaster's job covers a wide range of duties:

  • Managing the staff — supervising the postal workers, clerks, and delivery people who work at the post office.
  • Overseeing daily operations — making sure mail and parcels are sorted, processed, and dispatched correctly and on time.
  • Handling money matters — post offices often offer financial services (money orders, stamps, registered mail fees), and the postmaster is accountable for those transactions.
  • Dealing with customer issues — if something goes wrong — a lost parcel, a complaint — the postmaster is the authority people turn to.
  • Maintaining records — keeping track of deliveries, staffing, and finances.

In short, a postmaster is the head of a single post office branch, the same way a branch manager heads a bank branch.
The Historical Role (Important for Full Understanding)

The word "postmaster" has deep historical roots, and understanding the old role helps you fully grasp the modern one.

Centuries ago, before trains, cars, or telephones, the postal system was the backbone of all communication — for governments, armies, merchants, and ordinary people. Mail traveled by horse and rider. Along the long routes between cities and towns, there were posting stations (also called post houses) — stops where a tired horse could be swapped for a fresh one so the mail could keep moving without delay.

The postmaster of each of these stations had enormous responsibility. He kept the horses ready, managed the riders, received and dispatched mail bags, and kept records. He was often one of the most important and respected people in a town — someone appointed directly by the king or government. In many countries, the postmaster also served as an unofficial source of news, since all letters passed through his hands (and sometimes, he was legally permitted — or secretly paid — to read them on behalf of authorities).

So historically, a postmaster was not just an administrator. He was a critical node in the entire network of communication and power.

When you scale the concept upward — from a single post office to an entire country's postal system — you get the Postmaster General. This is the chief executive of a nation's postal service, overseeing tens of thousands of employees, offices, and the entire mail and parcel network.

For example, in the United States, the Postmaster General leads the United States Postal Service (USPS). In India, the Director General of Posts holds a similar top-level position (though the traditional title "Postmaster General" is also used at regional levels for senior postal officers overseeing a circle or zone).

Think of it this way:

  • Postmaster = manager of one post office.
  • Postmaster General = head of the entire national postal organization.

Historically, when a woman held this position, she was sometimes called a postmistress. This was common in the 18th and 19th centuries, especially in small towns where a widow or a woman might take over running the local post office. Today, the word postmaster is used regardless of gender.

In the modern world, the word has taken on a second life in computing and the internet.

When you send an email, it travels through mail servers — computer systems that route emails the way post offices route letters. The person (or the automated system) responsible for managing a mail server and keeping it running is also called a postmaster.

This is why, on almost every email domain, there exists a reserved address: postmaster@[domain].com. If you have a problem sending email to someone at that domain — say, your emails keep bouncing back — you can write to this address to report the issue to the technical administrator of that email system.

So "postmaster" in the digital world is a direct metaphor borrowed from the physical postal world: just as the postmaster of a post office handles problems with physical mail, the digital postmaster handles problems with electronic mail.

• "The postmaster informed the customers that the branch would be closed on the national holiday."
  • "In the 1800s, the local postmaster was one of the most well-connected people in any small town, since all correspondence passed through him."
  • "If your emails to that company keep bouncing, try writing to postmaster@theircompany.com."
  • "She was appointed postmaster of the district's largest sorting office after fifteen years of service."

A postmaster is the person in charge of a post office — historically a figure of great civic importance, today a branch manager of postal operations, and in the digital world, an administrator of an email server.
12555:
The adjective postmortem means "occurring after death" or "relating to something done or examined after death." When you place this word in front of a noun, it tells you that whatever that noun refers to — a report, an examination, a discovery — happened after a person or creature had already died.

The clearest and most classic example is the phrase postmortem examination. This is the medical procedure (also known as an autopsy) in which a doctor carefully inspects a dead body to find out the cause of death, the manner of death, or any hidden medical conditions. The examination cannot happen while the person is alive — by definition, it happens after death. That "after death" quality is exactly what the adjective postmortem is pointing to.
How It Works as an Adjective

As an adjective, postmortem always comes before a noun and modifies it. It answers the question: "When did this happen, or what period does this belong to?" The answer is always: after death.

Here are some phrases where it naturally appears in its literal, medical/legal sense:

  • Postmortem examination — the inspection of a body after death
  • Postmortem report — a written document that records what a doctor found during that examination
  • Postmortem interval — the amount of time that has passed between the moment of death and the moment the body is discovered or examined (used heavily in forensic science)
  • Postmortem changes — the physical changes a body undergoes after death (skin color change, stiffening of muscles, decomposition, etc.)
  • Postmortem lividity — the bluish-purple discoloration that appears on the skin where blood has pooled due to gravity, after the heart has stopped pumping
  • Postmortem findings — the things discovered and observed upon examining a dead body

In all of these, the word is doing one precise job: marking that something belongs to the period or process that follows death.
Shades and Nuances of the Literal Meaning

Even within its literal sense, the adjective captures a few related but distinct ideas:

1. Happening after death in time
Something that occurs simply because the person is now dead. For example, postmortem changes in the body begin immediately after the heart stops. These changes — like rigor mortis (stiffening of muscles) or decomposition — are described as postmortem because they are caused by or occur during the state of being dead.

2. Done after death for the purpose of understanding death
A postmortem examination or postmortem report is not just happening after death in time — it is specifically performed after death with the goal of understanding what happened. This is a deliberate human action taken in response to death.

The adjective covers both shades. Context usually makes clear which one is meant.

Over time, the word postmortem escaped the world of medicine and entered everyday language as a figurative adjective. Here, it no longer refers to a literal death — instead, it refers to the end of any event, process, or endeavor, treating that ending as if it were a death.

In this figurative sense, postmortem means: "occurring after the conclusion of something, typically involving a careful analysis of what went wrong or what happened."

Think of it this way: just as a doctor examines a dead body to understand what caused death, people figuratively "examine" a failed project, a lost game, a collapsed deal, or any concluded event to understand what caused its failure or shaped its outcome.

Examples:

  • Postmortem analysis — a careful review of a project, campaign, or event after it has ended, asking: "What went wrong? What went right? What can we learn?"
  • Postmortem meeting — a meeting held after a project fails (or even after it succeeds) to discuss what happened and extract lessons
  • Postmortem discussion — a conversation about an event after it is over and can no longer be changed
  • Postmortem review — a structured evaluation after the conclusion of something

You might hear this in business ("The team held a postmortem review after the product launch flopped"), in sports ("The coach conducted a postmortem analysis of the season"), in technology and software engineering (teams regularly schedule postmortem meetings after a system crash or failed release), and in politics or journalism ("Analysts began a postmortem examination of why the party lost the election").

Whether used literally or figuratively, the adjective postmortem always carries the same underlying logic:

Something has ended — permanently, irreversibly. What follows now belongs to the "postmortem" phase: the phase of looking back, examining, and understanding.

The literal use says: this person's life is over; we are now in the phase of examining what that ending means.

The figurative use says: this event or effort is over; we are now in the phase of examining what that ending means.

In both cases, the adjective marks a specific moment in time — the after — and assigns everything that happens in that after to its domain.
A Key Nuance: It Is Always Retrospective

One subtle but important quality of postmortem as an adjective is that it is inherently retrospective — it looks backward. You cannot plan a postmortem before the event ends. You can plan for one, but the postmortem analysis itself only becomes possible once the thing being analyzed is fully over.

This means the word also carries a quiet sense of finality. When something is described as requiring a postmortem examination (literal or figurative), it is acknowledging that what's done is done — there is no reversing it, no going back. The only thing left is to understand it.

To sharpen your understanding: compare postmortem with the word preliminary (meaning "before the main event"). These two sit on opposite ends of a timeline.

  • Preliminary examination → happens before the main event or conclusion
  • Postmortem examination → happens after death or conclusion

This contrast helps anchor the adjective clearly: it is firmly and always in the after.

Postmortem (adjective) = describing something that occurs or is done after death (literal sense) or after the end of an event or endeavor (figurative sense), usually with the purpose of examining, analyzing, or understanding what happened. It always implies finality — whatever is being examined is completely over — and it always looks backward in time.
12556:
A postmortem is an examination or analysis that happens after something has ended — most often after a death, or after an event has concluded. The key idea is: it always happens after the fact, looking backward to understand something more fully.

The word has two main lives — one in medicine, and one in everyday language.

In medicine, a postmortem (also called an autopsy) is a thorough, systematic examination of a dead body carried out by a doctor — specifically a type of specialist called a pathologist — to answer questions that couldn't be answered while the person was alive.

What is the doctor actually trying to find out?

The central question is almost always: "Why did this person die?"

But it can go deeper than that:

  • The cause of death — What biological event killed them? (e.g., a heart attack, a brain bleed, organ failure, poisoning)
  • The manner of death — Was it natural, accidental, a suicide, or a homicide?
  • The time of death — How long ago did the person die?
  • The progression of disease — If someone was sick, how far had the disease spread? Did it behave the way doctors expected?
  • Whether a treatment worked — In some cases, doctors want to know if a surgery or medication actually had the intended effect.

Who orders a postmortem?

  • A coroner or medical examiner (a legal official) orders one when a death is sudden, suspicious, unexplained, or violent — such as in a murder case, a road accident, or when someone dies alone and their body is found later.
  • A hospital might request one (with the family's permission) when a patient dies in ways that raise medical questions — for example, when doctors want to learn from a puzzling case.
  • A family can sometimes request one if they are unsatisfied with the given cause of death or want closure.

What actually happens during a medical postmortem?

The process is methodical and careful:

  1. The pathologist examines the outside of the body — noting injuries, marks, skin color, and other external signs.
  2. They open the body and examine internal organs one by one — the heart, lungs, liver, brain, kidneys, and so on — looking for damage, disease, abnormalities, or signs of trauma.
  3. They may take tissue samples and send them to a laboratory for microscopic analysis.
  4. They may also run toxicology tests — testing blood or urine for the presence of drugs, alcohol, or poisons.
  5. Finally, the pathologist writes a postmortem report, which is an official document detailing all findings and stating the official cause of death.

This report can be critically important in criminal trials, insurance claims, medical research, and helping families find answers.

Outside of medicine, the word postmortem is used very widely in everyday life to describe any serious, structured review that takes place after an event — usually one that went badly or ended unexpectedly.

The logic is borrowed directly from medicine: just as a pathologist examines a body to understand why it died, people "examine" a failed or completed event to understand why it unfolded the way it did.

Where you'll hear this used:

In business and project management:
After a project fails, is delayed, or ends — whether successfully or not — a team holds a postmortem meeting. They go through what happened step by step, asking:

  • What went wrong?
  • What went right?
  • What should we do differently next time?

This is extremely common in tech companies, where it's sometimes also called a "retrospective" or "lessons learned" session.

In politics and journalism:
After an election, especially a surprising or devastating loss, political analysts conduct a postmortem of the campaign. They analyze every decision — the messaging, the strategy, the resources — to explain the outcome.

In sports:
After a team suffers a shocking defeat, coaches and commentators perform a postmortem of the game — reviewing tactics, player decisions, and turning points.

In everyday conversation:
If you and your friends planned a party that went terribly, and then sat down the next day to discuss everything that went wrong so you never repeat the same mistakes — that casual conversation is, in spirit, a postmortem.

Whether it's medical or figurative, every postmortem shares these traits:

  1. It is backward-looking. It examines something that has already happened or already ended. You cannot do a postmortem on something that is still ongoing.
  2. It is analytical. It's not just talking about what happened — it's carefully digging into what happened to understand it at a deeper level.
  3. It seeks a specific kind of truth. In medicine: the cause of death. In general use: the cause of failure (or the reasons for an unexpected outcome).
  4. It has a purpose beyond the past. The insights gained from a postmortem are meant to inform the future — whether that's justice in a court of law, better medical knowledge, or smarter decisions next time.

• The word carries a serious tone. When someone says "let's do a postmortem," they are signaling that something significant happened and deserves careful attention — not a casual chat.
  • In the figurative sense, a postmortem is usually associated with negative events (failures, losses, disasters), though it can occasionally be used after any significant event to extract lessons.
  • A postmortem is not a blame session. Its purpose is understanding, not punishing. In professional settings especially, a good postmortem focuses on systems and decisions, not on attacking individuals.
  • The plural is simply postmortems.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
A postmortem is a careful, after-the-fact examination — of a dead body in medicine, or of a failed/concluded event in general life — conducted to understand why things turned out the way they did.
12557:
To postpone something means to move it to a later time than originally planned.

Think of it this way: you had a plan — a meeting at 3 PM today, a trip next Monday, an exam this Friday. Something comes up, or you make a decision, and now that event is going to happen later than you first intended. That act of pushing it forward in time is called postponing.

The single most important thing to understand about "postpone" is this: the event still happens — it just happens later. You are not canceling it. You are not abandoning it. You are buying more time before it takes place.
Postpone vs. Words That Look Similar

Because several words seem close in meaning, understanding how "postpone" differs from them is essential.

Postpone vs. Cancel
This is the biggest distinction. To cancel something means it will not happen at all — it is called off entirely. To postpone something means it will still happen, just at a different, later time. If a concert is cancelled, you will never see that show. If it is postponed, it has been moved to another date — the show will happen, just not today.

Postpone vs. Delay
These two words are very close in meaning and are often used interchangeably. The subtle difference is that "delay" can be unintentional — traffic can delay you, a storm can delay a flight. "Postpone," on the other hand, almost always describes a deliberate, conscious decision made by a person. You choose to postpone something. Also, "postpone" is slightly more formal than "delay."

Postpone vs. Put off
"Put off" is the everyday, informal way of saying the exact same thing as "postpone." If you say "I'll put off the dentist appointment," you mean the same thing as "I will postpone the dentist appointment." In casual speech, people lean toward "put off"; in formal or professional writing, "postpone" is preferred.

Postpone vs. Defer
"Defer" is also very similar and leans even more formal than "postpone." It is common in legal, financial, and official settings (e.g., "defer a payment," "defer a decision to a committee"). "Defer" can also carry the sense of handing responsibility over to someone else or waiting for a specific condition to be met. "Postpone" is more straightforwardly about moving something to a later time.

Postpone vs. Reschedule
When you reschedule something, you typically assign a new, specific date or time right away — you actively set a new appointment. When you postpone something, you may or may not know the new time yet. You might postpone a meeting to next week and already know the new slot, or you might postpone it without any specific new time in mind yet.
How It Is Used in Sentences

"Postpone" is a transitive verb, which means it needs an object — something that is being postponed.

Basic form:

  • We postponed the meeting.
  • She postponed her trip.
  • The government postponed the election.

With "until" to name the new time:

  • They postponed the match until Saturday.
  • He postponed the surgery until next month.
  • The conference was postponed until further notice.

With "by" to show how much time was added:

  • The launch was postponed by two weeks.
  • She postponed the deadline by three days.

With a gerund (verb + -ing) as the object:

  • He postponed making a decision.
  • They postponed announcing the results.

In the passive voice (very common, especially for official announcements):

  • The game has been postponed due to heavy rain.
  • The exam was postponed because of technical issues.

In the passive form, you focus on the event that was pushed back, without necessarily saying who made the decision. This is why you frequently see it written this way in news headlines and official statements.

In real life, "postpone" is used with a wide range of events and actions:

  • meetings, appointments, exams, elections, matches, games, concerts, surgeries, trials, summits, launches, decisions, payments, weddings, trips, announcements.

Basically, anything that was planned to happen at a specific time can be postponed.

Sometimes, when something is postponed, no new date is set. In this case, people say it has been "postponed indefinitely." This means: we are not sure when it will happen, and we are not committing to a new time right now. It is not the same as cancelled — officially, the event could still happen someday — but in practice, "postponed indefinitely" often signals that the chances of it happening are uncertain or slim.

"Postpone" is a moderately formal word. You will see it in news articles, official emails, business communication, and formal announcements. In everyday conversation with friends, you are more likely to say "put off" or "push back":

  • "Let's put off the trip." (casual)
  • "The meeting has been postponed." (formal/professional)

Both are grammatically correct and mean the same thing. Choosing between them is simply a matter of context and tone.
A Quick Mental Image to Remember It

Picture a timeline — a straight line moving from left (past) to right (future). You have a dot on that line marking when something is supposed to happen. To postpone means to pick up that dot and slide it further to the right. The dot doesn't disappear. It just moves later.

That's all "postpone" means: slide the event to the right on the timeline, by deliberate choice.
12558:
A postponement is the act of moving something from its original, planned time to a later time — intentionally, by someone's decision.

Think of it this way: something was supposed to happen at a specific time, but instead of happening then, it gets pushed forward in time. It will still happen — just later than originally planned.

Simple example: Your dentist appointment was on Monday at 10 AM. On Sunday night, the dentist calls and says she can't see you Monday — can you come on Thursday instead? That shift from Monday to Thursday is a postponement.
The Three Things That Must Be True

For something to be a postponement, three conditions must be present:

  1. Something was already planned. There was a specific time or date set for an event, meeting, task, or decision.
  2. It was deliberately moved back in time. Someone — a person, an organization, an authority — made the conscious decision to delay it.
  3. It will still happen — just later. It has not been abandoned or cancelled.

If any of these three are missing, it's not quite a postponement. For example, if your train is late because of heavy rain, that's a delay — not a postponement, because no one decided to push it back. And if your dentist cancels your appointment permanently with no rescheduling, that's a cancellation, not a postponement.
The Most Important Distinction: Postponement vs. Cancellation

This is the sharpest, most critical line to understand.

  • A postponement = "This will still happen, but at a different, later time."
  • A cancellation = "This will NOT happen at all."

When the Tokyo Olympics were moved from 2020 to 2021 due to the pandemic, that was a postponement — the games were delayed, but they still took place.

If the games had been called off entirely and never held, that would have been a cancellation.

This distinction matters a lot in real life. When someone hears "the concert is postponed," they know to keep their tickets — it's still coming. When they hear "the concert is cancelled," they ask for a refund.
The New Date: Known or Unknown?

A postponement doesn't always come with a new date immediately. There are two kinds:

  • Postponement with a new date: "The meeting has been postponed to November 15th." Here you know exactly when it will happen.
  • Open-ended postponement: "The trial has been postponed until further notice." Here it is confirmed that it will still happen, but the new date hasn't been decided yet.

Both are postponements. The second kind is sometimes called an indefinite postponement, meaning there's no clear timeline for when it will eventually occur.
What Postponement Implies About Intent

A postponement is always a deliberate act. When something is postponed, somebody chose to delay it. It might be because:

  • Circumstances changed (bad weather, illness, conflict)
  • More preparation is needed
  • Key people cannot attend
  • Resources aren't ready
  • External factors (like a government order) force the delay

Whatever the reason, the word "postponement" always carries the idea that someone made this call. It is not an accident; it is a decision.
How It's Used in Real Life — Contexts

Postponement appears across almost every area of life. Here are some common contexts where you'll encounter the word:

  • Events: A sports match, concert, wedding ceremony, or awards show can be postponed.
  • Meetings and sessions: A business meeting, a court hearing, a parliament session, or a school exam can be postponed.
  • Decisions: A judge might announce the postponement of a verdict. A company might announce the postponement of a decision on hiring.
  • Projects and launches: A rocket launch, a product release, or a construction project can face postponement.
  • Medical: A surgery or a medical procedure can be postponed.
  • Legal and official: Elections, trials, and policy implementations can be postponed.
Common Phrases and Collocations

In natural English, "postponement" appears frequently in these patterns:

  • "the postponement of [something]" → "the postponement of the elections," "the postponement of the meeting"
  • "announce a postponement" → to make the delay known publicly
  • "request a postponement" → to formally ask for more time before something happens
  • "grant a postponement" → to officially allow a delay that was requested
  • "due to the postponement" → explaining what happened as a result of the delay
  • "indefinite postponement" → a delay with no fixed new date
  • "repeated postponement" → when something is delayed again and again
The Noun in Action — Examples

To really cement the meaning, here are clear example sentences:

  1. The postponement of the cricket match disappointed thousands of fans who had already bought tickets.

(The match was moved to a later date; it wasn't cancelled.)

  1. She welcomed the postponement of her exam because she needed more time to study.

(The exam date was pushed forward; it will still happen later.)

  1. The court announced a postponement of the trial until January due to the judge's illness.

(The trial is delayed, not abandoned.)

  1. After three postponements, people started to wonder if the project would ever be completed.

(It had been delayed three times in a row — still not cancelled, but very delayed.)

  1. The indefinite postponement of the summit left world leaders uncertain about when they would meet.

(Delayed with no new date fixed yet.)
Repeated Postponements — An Important Real-World Note

Sometimes, something gets postponed not once but multiple times. Each delay is a separate postponement. Over time, repeated postponements can start to feel like a quiet cancellation — because even though the event is never officially called off, it never seems to actually happen either.

This is why "indefinite postponement" can sometimes be a polite or cautious way of saying something might not happen at all. Politicians, for instance, sometimes postpone controversial decisions again and again without ever cancelling them outright.
How It Relates to Similar Words

Understanding how "postponement" compares to near-synonyms helps sharpen your grasp of it:

  • Delay is broader and more general. A delay can be accidental (a traffic jam caused a delay) or intentional. Postponement is always intentional. Also, "postponement" is more formal.
  • Deferral is very close in meaning. It tends to appear in formal, legal, financial, or official contexts — "deferral of payment," "deferral of a decision." It's a slightly more technical word than postponement.
  • Adjournment specifically means the postponement of a formal session — like a court case, a parliament sitting, or a board meeting. When a judge says "court is adjourned," it means the proceedings are being paused and will resume later.
  • Rescheduling simply means setting a new time. It can mean moving something earlier OR later. Postponement specifically means moving it later.
  • Putting off or putting something on hold are informal, everyday expressions for the same idea as postponement.
The Word as a "Count" Noun

"Postponement" is a count noun, meaning you can talk about one postponement, two postponements, etc. You can refer to:

  • A single act of postponing: "The postponement was announced at noon."
  • Multiple instances: "There have been three postponements so far this year."
Summary in One Sentence
A postponement is a deliberate decision to move something from its planned time to a later time, with the understanding that it will still happen — just not when originally intended.
12559:
Postprandial is an adjective that simply means "happening after a meal."

If something is described as postprandial, it takes place, exists, or is measured in the period of time that follows eating — whether that meal is breakfast, lunch, or dinner.

That's the heart of it. Everything else below is just filling in the complete picture.
Breaking the Word Down (Without Getting Technical)

Think of the word in two parts:

  • "Post" — you already know this one. It means after, like "post-match interview" (interview after the match) or "postwar" (after the war).
  • "Prandial" — this simply refers to a meal.

Put them together: postprandial = after a meal. Simple.
Where and How It Is Used

The word "postprandial" shows up in two main worlds:

1. In Medicine and Science

This is where the word is most commonly and seriously used. Doctors and scientists frequently talk about what happens inside your body after you eat. Here, "postprandial" is a precise clinical term.

  • Postprandial blood sugar (glucose): Your blood sugar rises after you eat. Doctors measure your postprandial glucose level — meaning the amount of sugar in your blood after a meal — to check for conditions like diabetes.
  • Postprandial blood pressure: In some people, blood pressure drops shortly after eating. This is called postprandial hypotension.
  • Postprandial digestion: The entire process your gut goes through after a meal can be referred to as postprandial digestion.

In this world, the word is used with great precision. "Postprandial" in a medical report means specifically the phase after food has been consumed and your body is actively responding to it.

2. In Formal, Literary, or Elegant Writing

Outside of medicine, you'll find this word used in sophisticated writing or conversation to describe everyday after-meal activities — often with a slightly refined or even gently humorous tone. It lends a formal elegance to something quite ordinary.

  • A postprandial walk — a walk taken after a meal (many people do this to aid digestion or simply enjoy the habit).
  • A postprandial nap — a nap taken after eating.
  • Postprandial conversation — the relaxed chat that happens at the table after everyone has finished eating.
  • A postprandial drink — a drink (often something like brandy, coffee, or tea) enjoyed after a meal.

If someone says, "I enjoy a postprandial stroll through the park," they simply mean they like to go for a walk after eating. Using the word gives the sentence a polished, formal feel.

You know that heavy, sleepy feeling you get after a big meal? That's called postprandial somnolence — or more popularly, the postprandial dip (sometimes called a "food coma" in everyday speech).

After eating, your body diverts energy and blood flow toward digestion. Your blood sugar rises and then may dip. Some hormones that make you feel calm and sleepy are also released. The result is that drowsy, sluggish feeling in the hour or two after lunch or dinner. Scientists and doctors call this the postprandial dip, and it's a perfectly real and recognized physiological phenomenon.

This is probably the most relatable example of the word in action.

Since you now know "postprandial" (after a meal), it's worth knowing its direct opposite: preprandial, meaning before a meal.

  • A preprandial drink = a drink before eating (like an aperitif).
  • A preprandial blood sugar test = blood sugar measured before eating.

"Pre" means before, just as "post" means after.

ContextHow it's used
Doctors & researchersClinically and precisely — postprandial glucose, postprandial response
Writers & speakersFormally or stylishly — postprandial walk, postprandial chat
Everyday speechRarely — most people just say "after dinner"

Actually, let me just say it plainly: most ordinary people in daily conversation say "after dinner" or "after lunch." Postprandial lives mainly in medical writing, scientific research, and formal or literary prose. If you use it in conversation, you'll sound impressively well-read.

• "Her postprandial blood sugar was slightly elevated, so the doctor adjusted her medication."
  • "He had a pleasant postprandial walk along the river after Sunday lunch."
  • "The postprandial drowsiness hit him hard after the heavy pasta dinner."
  • "They sat in postprandial contentment, sipping tea and chatting lazily."

Postprandial means "occurring after a meal." It's used medically to describe your body's response to food, and in formal writing to describe relaxed after-meal habits like walks, naps, or conversations.
